rows: Food businesses must provide accurate information about specified allergens.
Allergen information is required for prepacked and non-prepacked food in applicable forms.
Ingredients and recipes should be controlled so allergen information remains current.
Cross-contact risk should be assessed and reduced through suitable controls.
Staff need training to handle allergen enquiries and orders safely.
Changes in suppliers, ingredients or processes should trigger information review.
Precautionary allergen labelling should reflect a genuine residual risk assessment.
Incidents and near misses should trigger investigation and corrective action.
An allergen matrix or 'may contain' statement does not prove that allergen risk is controlled.
Conclusions require recipe, ingredients, supplier data, cross-contact controls, staff practice, label and change-management evidence.
Food businesses should be able to identify from whom food was supplied and to whom it was supplied.
Traceability records should accurately identify products and business partners.
Records should be accessible without undue delay.
Batch, lot and date information can support effective traceability.
Internal traceability improves the speed and precision of product action.
Supplier and customer details should remain linked to relevant products.
Traceability arrangements should be tested and reviewed.
Records support withdrawals, recalls and incident investigation.
A batch code or invoice alone may not reconstruct a complete product chain.
Conclusions require product identity, lot, quantity, supplier, customer, dates, internal movement and record-access evidence.
Unsafe food should be withdrawn from the supply chain.
A consumer recall is required when unsafe food may have reached consumers and recall is necessary.
Food businesses should notify the competent authority when required.
Traceability records should define the affected product and distribution.
Risk assessment should inform the scope and urgency of action.
Customers and consumers should receive clear, accurate information.
Recovered stock should be controlled and accounted for.
Effectiveness should be checked and lessons incorporated into corrective action.
Issuing a notice or removing stock from one site does not prove that a withdrawal or recall is complete.
Conclusions require hazard, affected lots, distribution, notification, consumer communication, recovery, reconciliation and effectiveness evidence.
Clostridium botulinum can grow and produce toxin in suitable anaerobic food conditions.
Vacuum packing and modified-atmosphere packing can create low-oxygen conditions.
Chilled shelf life should be supported by validated controls.
Factors such as acidity, salt, water activity, heat treatment and temperature can inhibit growth.
Businesses should identify botulism as a relevant hazard where applicable.
Cold-chain control should be maintained and monitored.
Process changes or shelf-life extension require reassessment.
Suspected botulism or loss of control requires urgent product and public-health action.
A vacuum seal or refrigerated label does not prove that botulism risk is controlled.
Conclusions require product formulation, process, pack atmosphere, shelf life, temperature, validation, monitoring and incident evidence.
